chapters.title: One Person, Several Desks
chapters.tease: A solo agency is one person at four desks. Agents now staff the production desk; the other three stay yours.

chapters.title: Not a Freelancer, Not a Consultant
chapters.tease: Freelancers sell hours, consultants sell advice. An agency sells a named outcome, delivered by a system.

chapters.title: What Changed When the Agents Arrived
chapters.tease: Production became very cheap. Judgement, trust and hard conversations cost exactly what they always did.

chapters.title: The Clients Do Not Care How
chapters.tease: Clients buy outcomes. Make the work so consistently good they never wonder how it was made, and never hide it.

chapters.title: Judgement Up, Production Down
chapters.tease: Production goes down to the agents. Judgement stays up with you. Checking is shared.

chapters.title: The Operating Model on a Napkin
chapters.tease: A solo agency is a loop of four stations: offer, pipeline, delivery and money, checked once a week.

chapters.title: The Myth of Infinite Capacity
chapters.tease: Agents scale output, not your attention. Capacity is set by how many clients you can hold in your head.

chapters.title: Small on Purpose
chapters.tease: Staying small can be a strategy, not a waiting room. With agents it is more viable than ever.

chapters.title: Your First Honest Audit
chapters.tease: Log one honest week, tag every hour as judgement, relationship or production, and see where time really goes.

chapters.title: The Edge Is Taste and Trust
chapters.tease: When production is cheap for everyone, the edge is taste and trust. Headcount is not.

chapters.title: Sell a Result, Not a Menu
chapters.tease: Clients arrive knowing what is wrong, not what they need. Sell the result they will have, not your menu.

chapters.title: Pick a Buyer You Can Find
chapters.tease: An offer without a buyer is a hobby. Choose a buyer you can name, find and reach without heroic effort.

chapters.title: Problems That Recur
chapters.tease: Recurring problems bring recurring revenue, and each month the cost to deliver falls while the value rises.

chapters.title: The Productised Offer
chapters.tease: A productised offer is a service shaped like a product: named, fixed scope, fixed time, fixed fee.

chapters.title: Naming the Thing
chapters.tease: Name the offer plainly and specifically, in the buyer's own words, so clients can repeat it without you.

chapters.title: Scope Is a Fence, Not a Wish
chapters.tease: Draw the boundary in advance, calmly, in words specific enough to check. Do not discover it mid-project.

chapters.title: The Ladder of Offers
chapters.tease: Give clients three rungs: a small entry offer, a core productised offer, and an ongoing retainer.

chapters.title: Cheap to Make, Not Cheap to Buy
chapters.tease: When agents cut your cost, keep the price. Anchor fees to the result's value, not the hours it took.

chapters.title: Saying What You Do Not Do
chapters.tease: Say what you do not do. Exclusions give the offer a shape and protect the delivery machine.

chapters.title: Sell It Before You Build It
chapters.tease: Describe the offer on one page and ask real buyers to buy it, with money, before you build it properly.

chapters.title: Pipeline Is a Habit
chapters.tease: Treat the pipeline as a weekly habit, not a panic when work runs low. Small, steady actions compound.

chapters.title: Referrals Are Earned in Delivery
chapters.tease: Referrals are not luck. They are earned in delivery, when working with you makes the client proud.

chapters.title: Findable for One Thing
chapters.tease: Be known for one thing by one group, and say the same specific sentence everywhere buyers look.

chapters.title: Writing That Sells Quietly
chapters.tease: Agents can write the sentences. Only your point of view, from real client work, gives anyone a reason to read.

chapters.title: Outreach Without the Spam
chapters.tease: Few messages, each researched and worth reading. Relevance, research and restraint beat volume.

chapters.title: The Discovery Call
chapters.tease: A discovery call is not a pitch. Ask, listen and diagnose; the client should do most of the talking.

chapters.title: Qualifying Out
chapters.tease: A bad-fit client costs far more than their fee. Spot misfits early and let them go before anyone invests.

chapters.title: A CRM You Will Actually Use
chapters.tease: A CRM has one job for a solo agency: nothing falls through the cracks. Keep it simple enough to use.

chapters.title: Partners Who Send Work
chapters.tease: Your buyers' other suppliers can send you warm work, if referring you always makes them look good.

chapters.title: The Feast-Famine Brake
chapters.tease: Stopping marketing during a feast schedules the next famine. A small weekly minimum is the brake.

chapters.title: The Proposal Is a Mirror
chapters.tease: A proposal should mirror the client's situation in their own words before it says anything about you.

chapters.title: Three Options, One Recommendation
chapters.tease: Offer three real options so the question becomes which, not whether. Then say which you recommend, and why.

chapters.title: Write the Definition of Done
chapters.tease: Write a short, checkable definition of done, so projects end cleanly instead of drifting into tweaks.

chapters.title: Assumptions Are Load-Bearing
chapters.tease: Every plan stands on assumptions. Write them down, each with a calm consequence, so nobody argues later.

chapters.title: Agents Draft, You Decide
chapters.tease: Agents draft the proposal in minutes. The recommendation, assumptions, framing and fee stay with you.

chapters.title: Speed Is a Feature
chapters.tease: A proposal the next morning previews how delivery will feel. Ten days later, the momentum has gone.

chapters.title: Following Up Without Grovelling
chapters.tease: Silence after a proposal is normal. Follow up three times, each with something useful, then let it go.

chapters.title: The Price Conversation
chapters.tease: Raise money on the discovery call with a range, not at the end. State the fee plainly, like a fact.

chapters.title: When They Want It Cheaper
chapters.tease: When a client wants it cheaper, change what they are buying, not what it is worth.

chapters.title: The Signature Is the Start
chapters.tease: The client's doubt starts the moment they sign. An immediate, organised sequence gives it nothing to feed on.

chapters.title: Onboarding Is Expectation Management
chapters.tease: The first fortnight sets the tone. Onboarding is expectation management: say it early, in writing.

chapters.title: The Welcome Pack
chapters.tease: One document, sent within a day of signing, answering the first month's questions before they become worries.

chapters.title: The Login Hunt
chapters.tease: Treat access and assets as a planned workstream, requested in one list on day one, not an afterthought.

chapters.title: The Kickoff Call
chapters.tease: A kickoff should end in decisions, not just enthusiasm. Agenda first, decisions read out, follow-up same day.

chapters.title: The Client Brief File
chapters.tease: One living file per client holds the context a person or an agent needs to do work that fits.

chapters.title: One Channel, Not Seven
chapters.tease: Choose one primary channel per client, say so at the start, and redirect politely every time.

chapters.title: The First Visible Win
chapters.tease: Deliver something small, real and useful in the first week or two. Early proof turns anxiety into confidence.

chapters.title: Explaining How You Work
chapters.tease: Explain once, early and plainly, that agents produce and you direct and check. Then let the work talk.

chapters.title: Mapping the Stakeholders
chapters.tease: Map everyone who matters by influence and involvement, early, and find the person nobody has mentioned.

chapters.title: The Two-Week Check-In
chapters.tease: Two weeks in, ask how the relationship is working, not what you have done. Small fixes now beat repairs later.

chapters.title: A System, Not Heroics
chapters.tease: A delivery system that holds on a bad day beats a talented owner pulling late nights.

chapters.title: Playbooks as Code
chapters.tease: Write each playbook like code: specific, modular, versioned and tested, so an agent can run it.

chapters.title: The Brief Is the Product
chapters.tease: The quality of agent work is capped by the brief, so briefing is where your judgement enters the product.

chapters.title: Templates, Skills and Parts
chapters.tease: Every delivery should make the next one cheaper, by turning repeated work into a library of reusable parts.

chapters.title: One Conductor, Many Hands
chapters.tease: Many agents need one conductor: decompose the work, track it in one place, and integrate before review.

chapters.title: Where the Human Must Touch
chapters.tease: Agents produce between three explicit human checkpoints, and the final review is never optional.

chapters.title: Version Everything
chapters.tease: Keep a history of every change, with approvals marked, so any change can be undone in one step.

chapters.title: Client Data and the Agent
chapters.tease: Match each AI tool to the sensitivity of the client data, and share as little data as the job needs.

chapters.title: Tools Without Tool Worship
chapters.tease: Choose tools by the job they do, master the ones you have, and change one tool at a time.

chapters.title: Measuring Throughput Honestly
chapters.tease: Measure cycle time, rework and your own hours; agent volume flatters but rarely tells the truth.

chapters.title: Defined Before It Is Checked
chapters.tease: Quality must be written down as specific, checkable criteria before anyone, human or agent, can aim at it.

chapters.title: The Two-Pass Review
chapters.tease: Every deliverable gets two reviews: an agent against the written standard, then you against the client.

chapters.title: Spotting the Machine Sheen
chapters.tease: Fluent but empty agent prose, the machine sheen, is removed by adding what only this client would recognise.

chapters.title: Checklists for the Embarrassing
chapters.tease: A short pre-delivery checklist, run by an agent then by you, catches cheap errors that cost the most trust.

chapters.title: The Update Nobody Asked For
chapters.tease: A short, regular update sent before the client asks removes almost all the worry that silence creates.

chapters.title: Bad News Travels First
chapters.tease: Tell the client about a problem the day you know, with a plan, before they discover it themselves.

chapters.title: Feedback Rounds With Edges
chapters.tease: Agree feedback rounds with edges: one consolidated voice, set rounds and timing, then change requests.

chapters.title: The Unhappy Client
chapters.tease: With an unhappy client, listen, own it and repair it, then find the gap in your system that caused it.

chapters.title: Outcomes, Not Activity
chapters.tease: Report what changed for the client first; the list of activity is only the receipt.

chapters.title: The Case Study Habit
chapters.tease: Capture situation, decisions, results and a client quote during the work, so case studies take minutes.

chapters.title: Cash Is the Oxygen
chapters.tease: A profitable agency can still run out of cash, so forecast it weekly and defend the low point early.

chapters.title: Deposits and Milestones
chapters.tease: Take a deposit before work starts and invoice at milestones, so you never fund a client’s project for them.

chapters.title: Invoicing Like a Machine
chapters.tease: Invoice like a machine: the same day, the same format, every requirement right, approved in seconds.

chapters.title: The Retainer Done Right
chapters.tease: A good retainer buys a defined monthly result, billed in advance, not a block of your hours.

chapters.title: Pricing Value Without Apology
chapters.tease: Set the fee as a modest share of the value created, check it clears your cost floor, and never apologise.

chapters.title: Margins When Making Is Cheap
chapters.tease: When agents make production cheap, margin is what you choose to keep, not what is left by default.

chapters.title: The Runway
chapters.tease: Runway, the months you could survive with no new income, decides whether you choose from fear or freedom.

chapters.title: Chasing Late Payment Calmly
chapters.tease: Chase late payment with a calm, escalating sequence that an agent runs and you approve.

chapters.title: No Is a Financial Decision
chapters.tease: Every yes spends scarce capacity, so test each opportunity against written criteria before saying it.

chapters.title: Raising Prices Gracefully
chapters.tease: Raise prices on two tracks: new fees for new clients at once, and notice before renewal for existing ones.

chapters.title: The Contract Is a Kindness
chapters.tease: A contract records what was agreed while everyone is friendly, so it can settle things when they are not.

chapters.title: Who Owns What
chapters.tease: Clients own the deliverables they paid for; you keep the templates and methods; a licence covers the overlap.

chapters.title: Liability, Insurance and Sleep
chapters.tease: Four layers stand between a claim and your home: records, insurance, a liability cap and company structure.

chapters.title: Scope Creep Has a Paper Trail
chapters.tease: Route every extra request through a light change note, so scope grows only by informed, recorded consent.

chapters.title: Office Hours for One
chapters.tease: Publish office hours and response times, keep them consistently, and let an agent acknowledge after hours.

chapters.title: The Always-On Trap
chapters.tease: Agents can work overnight; your attention should not follow them. Review the output in the morning.

chapters.title: Holidays Are a Process
chapters.tease: Treat a holiday as a three-phase process, before, during and after, and time away becomes routine.

chapters.title: Burnout Arrives Quietly
chapters.tease: Burnout arrives gradually; a weekly energy score shows the slide, and the cure is fixing the business design.

chapters.title: The Bus Factor of One
chapters.tease: Your bus factor is one, so write a short continuity document that lets someone else steady things.

chapters.title: Firing a Client
chapters.tease: Ask whether you would take the client on today; if not, exit kindly with an excellent handover.

chapters.title: Should You Hire at All
chapters.tease: Before hiring, name what you are short of; only a shortage of judgement truly points to a person.

chapters.title: The First Human Is a Contractor
chapters.tease: Make your first human collaborator a contractor, and let trust build from a small project to a partnership.

chapters.title: Hire for Judgement, Not Hands
chapters.tease: Agents now supply the hands, so any hire should bring judgement: directing agents and catching what is wrong.

chapters.title: Agents Before Employees
chapters.tease: Exhaust what agents and systems can do before hiring, so any person you add is there for judgement or cover.

chapters.title: Growth Without Headcount
chapters.tease: A solo agency grows by raising the value of each hour through five levers, not by adding people.

chapters.title: The Brand of One
chapters.tease: Clients hire you, not a logo, so the same person must show up at every touchpoint, agent-assisted or not.

chapters.title: Taste Is Trained
chapters.tease: Taste is not a gift but a practice: see widely, choose, explain why, test it and cut.

chapters.title: Trust Compounds Slowly
chapters.tease: Trust builds slowly from small kept promises, lets clients stop checking, and can vanish in one breach.

chapters.title: The Agency in Five Years
chapters.tease: Hold tools lightly and invest in what endures: clients, taste, judgement, relationships and clear writing.

chapters.title: Taste and Trust, Not Headcount
chapters.tease: A solo agency’s edge is taste and trust; everything else is machinery, and headcount is only a means.
